title: Dichotomy of Feature Learning and Unlearning: Fast-Slow Analysis on Neural Networks with Stochastic Gradient Descent
claim: Fast-slow dynamics along a critical manifold explain why training either keeps learning features or gradually loses them.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right; phase portrait then two time-series, red/blue color coding
description: Three panels share a red and blue color code. The left panel is a phase-space plot on a gray background. The x-axis is first-layer alignment R_τ and the y-axis is second-layer weight a_τ. A thick green S-shaped critical manifold runs across it. Two trajectories start on the y-axis at ā, one red and one blue. Dotted horizontal arrows show fast dynamics. Solid arrows show slow motion along the manifold. The red path ends at a green dot, labeled feature learning. The blue path heads up and to the left, labeled feature unlearning. A legend box explains solid versus dotted arrows. The middle panel plots alignment R_τ against time τ. The red curve rises in staircase jumps, and the blue curve peaks and then decays toward zero. The right panel plots test loss against time. The red curve drops in steps, and the blue curve flattens at a higher level.
caption: Fast-slow dynamics of first-layer alignment (𝑅𝜏) and second-layer weights (𝑎𝜏) in time 𝜏, explaining the evolution of alignment and test loss. In the space of 𝑅𝜏 and 𝑎𝜏, the 𝑅−𝑎space in the left panel, we find a critical manifold (green curve). Each trajectory starts from its initial point (0, ¯𝑎) and, after reaching the manifold, slowly evolves along it. On all panels, the red trajectory represents feature learning, while the blue trajectory represents feature unlearning. The solid line represents slow dynamics, and the dashed line represents fast dynamics. In the feature learning case, test loss decreases like a staircase when |𝑅𝜏| increases via the fast dynamic. In the feature unlearning case, |𝑅𝜏| initially increases, then converges to zero due to the slow dynamics on the manifold.
abstract: The dynamics of gradient-based training in neural networks often exhibit nontrivial structures; hence, understanding them remains a central challenge in theoretical machine learning. In particular, a concept of feature unlearning, in which a neural network progressively loses previously learned features over long training, has gained attention. In this study, we consider the infinite-width limit of a two-layer neural network updated with a large-batch stochastic gradient, then derive differential equations with different time scales, revealing the mechanism and conditions for feature unlearning to occur. Specifically, we utilize the fast-slow dynamics: while an alignment of first-layer weights develops rapidly, the second-layer weights develop slowly. The direction of a flow on a critical manifold, determined by the slow dynamics, decides whether feature unlearning occurs. We give numerical validation of the result, and derive theoretical grounding and scaling laws of the feature unlearning. Our results yield the following insights: (i) the strength of the primary nonlinear term in data induces the feature unlearning, and (ii) an initial scale of the second-layer weights mitigates the feature unlearning. Technically, our analysis utilizes Tensor Programs and the singular perturbation theory.
